items: Grove serves students learning alongside a course.
Grove works for learners at any level, beginner to advanced.
The learner sets objectives with weight sliders across skills (reading, listening, vocabulary, grammar, writing); the sliders steer what comes automatically.
The learner picks a topic, and texts are about it.
A topic brings its own new words into the learner's tree.
The learner can paste an article on a topic.
New material is mostly what the learner already knows, with at most 1 new word or phrase per sentence (the target; PR-p1-130 sets how far an AI answer may miss it).
The share of known words in a text starts at 95%.
The share of known words moves with the learner's ratings, between 93% and 98%.
Grammar patterns are tracked as items, alongside words and phrases.
Items form a dependency tree: words unlock phrases, phrases unlock patterns.
The learner sees their knowledge as a growing tree/graph (visual map).
Known items reappear in new contexts, instead of plain flashcard review.
Difficulty rises automatically as knowledge grows.
A word or phrase counts as learned when it's in the learner's ground.
The learner can mark any ground item for drilling later.
Only drilled items have a spaced-repetition strength and can fade.
Grammar patterns keep plain spaced repetition.
Learners can add items (words, phrases, patterns) themselves.
The AI generates items from what the learner knows.
Items are extracted from texts the learner pastes in.
No paid tier in v1; a paid tier may come later.
The AI (by copy-paste) generates reading texts.
The AI gives meanings for unknown words in pasted texts.
The AI gives starter vocabulary for topics.
There is no conversation partner in the first version.
Grammar patterns are shown as a short rule plus examples.
Grammar patterns are colour-coded inside sentences.
The app runs in a desktop web browser.
The app works on phones (phone-friendly web).
A small server stores the data; a database is fine.
AI isn't required on the server.
Sentences have a play button that reads them aloud with the browser's built-in voices.
The learner can always choose which type of exercise to do from the home page, whatever the sliders say.
The first version costs nothing to run beyond the owner's Claude Pro: no paid AI API.
Learners copy a prompt from grove into their own AI chat and paste the answer back.
Each AI feature shows a 'Copy prompt' button and a paste box.
The prompts work in any chat AI.
The prompts ask for one JSON block (a fixed data format), which grove reads exactly.
When a pasted answer is malformed or breaks the rules, grove lists the problems.
Grove gives a 'fix it' message to paste back into the same AI chat.
AI (copy-paste or own key) is required for the main flow: reading passages always come from the AI; grove has no built-in passage generator.
One content package is about an hour of input.
By default a package comes in parts of about 20 minutes, one prompt each.
Closely bound content (e.g. consecutive episodes) stays in the same part.
Grove gives a 'next part' prompt until the package is complete.
The learner picks the mix of a package before copying the prompt.
Story series: the AI invents the characters.
The learner asks for a series topic or chooses from options.
Each episode reuses the last episode's new words.
After a text, questions in simple Swedish check understanding.
New words are explained in simple Swedish.
English is shown only on tap.
English is hidden completely above a level the learner chooses.
After each text the learner rates how much they understood on five buttons.
A rating of 'almost nothing' or 'a little' leads to fewer new words and shorter sentences.
After such a rating, grove offers a simpler retelling of the text.
Several 'most' or 'everything' ratings in a row lead to slightly more new words.
A text counts as understood when rated 'most' or 'everything'.
Listening: the learner can listen first and see the text afterwards.
Speech can be slower or normal speed.
The sentence being read is highlighted.
One sentence can be played on a loop.
A whole text can be played audio-only.
Grove tracks hours of input (reading and listening).
Grove counts how many times the learner has met each word.
Grove shows an estimated CEFR level from the ground.
Spaced repetition applies only to words and phrases the learner marks for drilling.
A drilled item joins the ground when drilling succeeds.
Meeting words in texts is counted and shown but doesn't change their schedule.
The sliders alone decide how much input and how much drilling the learner gets.
Prompts ask the AI to reuse the learner's fading words in new texts.
Grove explains comprehensible input in a way that motivates learners and convinces them of the approach.
After new content arrives, the learner marks the words they don't know, only half know, or never remember.
A dictionary lists every word, phrase and grammar pattern the learner has met.
Each dictionary entry shows its translation.
Each dictionary entry shows an example of where the learner met it.
Sentences from accepted AI texts are saved and reused in later exercises.
Texts the learner pastes are saved (without English).
The learner's data is saved after every change.
Each sentence shows how many new words it has.
Each text shows its word count, its new words and their share.
Clicking any word opens an inspector.
Unknown words can be added from the inspector.
The inspector shows the word's meaning, status and strength.
The inspector shows the phrases and patterns the word is part of.
Character and place names have their own list and never count as new words.
Listening mode blurs the text until clicked.
English translations can be shown or hidden.
Multiple choice asks for a word's meaning inside a sentence, not on its own.
A drilled word joins the ground after a correct answer once its review interval reaches 4 days.
A drilled word counts as fading when its strength drops below 0.2.
Meeting a grammar pattern in a text gives it a light review (patterns only).
Input time per text counts at most three times its estimated length and at least 30 seconds.
The fix-it message lists the exact sentences and words that broke the rules.
Prompts ask the AI for inflected forms of known words; grove learns them so they stop counting as unknown.
New words from an accepted text, grammar example or topic go straight into the tree as new, with the AI's meaning.
AI grammar explanations are saved with the pattern.
The examples in AI grammar explanations are reused in exercises.
Unit lengths: about 5 min per episode, 4 per retelling, 4 per dialogue, 6 per choose-your-path story.
Default package mix: 4 episodes, 2 retellings, 3 dialogues, 2 choose-your-path stories.
The whole package can be asked for in one prompt instead of in parts.
Five preset series ideas to choose from, plus your own topic.
Estimated CEFR level from known words: A1 250, A2 750, B1 1500, B2 3000, C1 6000, C2 10000.
Progress shows minutes of input per day.
Progress shows the ground over time (from daily snapshots).
Progress compares each skill's share of practice with its slider.
Locked items (parts not yet known) are shown with dashed outlines on the map.
A welcome screen on the first visit.
The server collects a large bank of words and grammar for each language.
Bank entries have translations, examples and inflections.
Clicking a known word opens the word inspector, which has a 'Drill this' button (how PR-p1-12's 'mark for drilling later' works).
Several learners, each with an account and login.
Speech starts at normal speed (1×); the learner can change it in Settings (PR-p1-76).
Bank entries come from the AI answers learners paste in.
Bank entries come from open dictionaries such as Wiktionary (licences to check).
The owner can write or correct bank entries.
The bank (PR-p1-89) is shared by all learners on the server.
Grove uses the bank for word meanings without asking the AI each time.
Grove uses the bank to recognise inflected forms, so they don't count as unknown.
Grove uses the bank for example sentences in exercises.
Grove uses the bank to check AI answers.
New entries for the shared bank are checked by a background process; until checked, other learners don't get them.
The learner who pasted an answer can use its new words right away, marked 'unchecked' until the background check passes.
Anyone can sign up for an account.
The background check (PR-p1-97) compares a new entry with an open dictionary imported into the bank (e.g. Wiktionary).
Only the owner can approve entries for everyone, in a review list; a teacher's approval stays within their class (PR-p1-105).
An entry that disagrees with the dictionary goes to the owner's review list; until the owner decides, only the learner who pasted it has it, marked 'unchecked'.
An entry the dictionary doesn't have goes to the owner's review list; until the owner decides, only the learner who pasted it has it, marked 'unchecked'.
Translations in the bank are into English only for now.
When the owner rejects an entry, they can offer a correction or deletion.
The learner who pasted a rejected entry chooses: keep it marked 'rejected', or take what the owner offers.
A new learner can pick their CEFR level; grove adds the most common words for that level to their ground.
After picking a level, grove shows a sample of words from that level; the learner ticks the ones they don't know, and the rest of the level's words join the ground (known by default).
A learner who doesn't know their level takes a reading test: short texts that get harder, each rated on the five buttons (PR-p1-33); that sets their level.
The starting level also sets which grammar patterns count as known.
The list of words ranked by how common they are (frequency list) lives in the shared bank for each language (PR-p1-89, PR-p1-110).

An 'Expand your grove' exercise, available any time: grove shows the next most common words not yet in the ground (from the frequency list, PR-p1-119); the learner ticks the ones they don't know, and the rest join the ground.
Grove offers 'Expand your grove' on its own when texts start having very few new words.
Grove offers 'Expand your grove' on its own after a certain amount of input (e.g. every 2 hours).
'Expand your grove' mixes in a few words already in the ground; ticking one as unknown takes it out of the ground and starts drilling it (catches wrong guesses from the starting level).
Words not in the ground that the learner ticks as unknown in the starting check or in 'Expand your grove' stay 'new' and come up in texts; they aren't drilled.
Each grammar pattern's level (e.g. 'verb second' is A1) is stored with the pattern in the shared bank.
The AI suggests a pattern's level when it's first added.
Now and then, texts below the learner's level are mixed in with normal ones.
The learner can ask for an easy read: a text below their level.
Grove's processing and storage run on the owner's own computer; a public relay server passes traffic between learners and it.
The owner can copy the review list as one prompt for their own AI and paste the verdicts back; grove applies them.
When the owner's computer is off, grove is unavailable until it's back.
Grove accepts an AI answer without a fix-it round when at most about 1 sentence in 10 has 2 new words; the exact margin is set after testing with real answers.
Grove accepts an AI answer without a fix-it round when the text as a whole is within about 2 percentage points of the target share of known words; the exact margin is set after testing.
Texts learners get from their AI are offered, after the background check, to other learners at a similar level (a shared library).
The background check of a text for the shared library covers the whole text and all its words.
One prompt can ask the AI for a week's worth of texts, pasted back in parts; meant mainly for learners whose AI gives long answers in one go.
The automatic check of bank entries also uses other free online dictionaries.
The automatic check looks for the word in real use (example sentences) in open text collections (corpora, e.g. Språkbanken's).
Word tiles, fill the gap and type the translation work without AI, from saved sentences and the bank.
A text the learner pasted from elsewhere (not written by their AI) goes into the shared library only when the learner confirms it may be shared.
Grove keeps the source of every library text: who shared it, and where it came from.
If a library text breaks copyright, the owner can delete it; the words it added to the bank stay.
The learner chooses, for each text, whether it goes into the shared library.
Texts a learner shares get a higher priority in the background check, so they're confirmed sooner.
The learner who shared a text chooses whether it shows their name or stays anonymous.
Any learner can report a library text as breaking copyright, wrong or offensive.
Learners accept terms of use when they sign up; among other things, they may only share texts they have the right to share.
When a library text is deleted for copyright, the example sentences taken from it are deleted too; only its words stay in the bank.
The first time an account shares a text that breaks copyright, it is suspended for a fixed period (e.g. 30 days); the suspension then lifts by itself.
The second time, the account is banned.
Only copyright breaches lead to suspension or a ban; offensive or wrong texts are just deleted.
There is exactly one owner, set in grove's settings on the owner's computer; nobody can become owner through grove.
Everyone who signs up is a learner.
The owner doesn't see learners' progress inside courses.
Every request is checked on the server against who is asking and their role.
After 5 failed sign-ins in a row, the account is locked for 15 minutes.
Passwords are stored hashed (scrambled), never as written.
Each account can add only a limited number of new bank entries a day.
Every change to the shared bank is logged with who made it, when and what.
Sign-ups per hour from one place are limited.
A single paste has a maximum size.
Visitors who aren't signed in reach only the sign-in and sign-up pages and public information; everything else needs an account.

notes.170: Articles only if they aren't under copyright.
notes.6: Applies to AI-generated material only; pasted material needs a separate solution. The exact number of new items per sentence is still to be decided.
notes.176: Grammar patterns can go to the ground too; how a pattern gets there is still open.
